claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are governed by interactions between local chemical ordering and dislocation activity.
The electronic structure of a high-entropy alloy influences local chemical ordering and dislocation activity.
Controlled elemental additions and processing changes can vary alloy composition and microstructure.
Local chemical ordering and dislocation density are the proposed structural mediators.
Electronic structure influences the formation of local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering affects dislocation activity.
Changes in dislocation activity consequently alter hardness and strength.
A higher degree of local chemical ordering is expected to produce higher hardness and strength.
Lower dislocation density is expected to produce higher hardness and strength.
Random-solid-solution high-entropy alloys with minimal local chemical ordering provide the proposed baseline.
The proposed relationships are expected to apply only over a limited range of composition and microstructure.
Outside that range, grain-boundary strengthening or precipitation hardening may dominate.
Different processing conditions and compositions can generate varying degrees of local chemical ordering and dislocation density.
Failure of hardness and strength to follow the predicted trends with local chemical ordering and dislocation density would falsify the hypothesis.
